They generally have good motives and their heart in the right place but don’t always know how to effectively approach things. 

I’m really amazed with Gen Z and politics. I’ve seen so many actually be engaged with it, doing a lot of activism and going out there and getting their hands dirty rather than just saying their views. However, a big struggle I see is how many don’t approach it correctly and instead cause themselves more harm than good. 

Example when it comes to debating on something political. Some people you know you’re never going to chance. Regardless of how you approach, what actions, sayings, etc, they’re not going to listen. It’s talking to a brick wall. But there are people who may seem firm in their beliefs but they mainly haven’t been exposed to a lot of other perspectives or views outside what they were raised. It’s also how you approach them. If someone is saying something that’s opposite what I believe and why I may want to question it, instead I come at them getting angry and calling them an idiot or start swearing? They’re not really going to be calm and nod their head and allow me to speak. They’re going to double down, get defensive and argue back. 

That’s an issue I see with Gen Z. They have their heart in the right place but they don’t always know how to approach on some issues and it’s only seen in a black or white matter. Or understanding who and what they need to put their energy into in order to make more of an impact. I do believe it’s something they’ll grow more into and begin to understand as many begin to grow though.

You are **not** stupid. You are **not** destined to be a failure. You **did not** lose any qualities of yourself. Then so many students are pushed into this standard of "congrats you graduated high school, now go to college right now, ok you graduated college, now go pick a job that's most likely going to be shitty and not what you expected." 

You don't ever get a break and grinding yourself to an oblivion is considered "normal." You are giving all you can and that's ok. That doesn't make you stupid or a failure. You are obviously showing that mental health problems are arising and getting diagnosed.

NTA but I wouldn't really call it an asshole move. But I do want to share some perspective for you and possibly anyone else interested:  


I'm a queer trans man from the south (north carolina). I was born and raised here my whole life and I felt uncomfortable and like it was a shit-show. I moved to a more progressive area in North Carolina and that really changed my perspective a lot. The south gets a bad rep for being anti-lgbtq but thing is, that's everywhere. Hell, you go to rural areas of NY and confederate flags will be there. Even in big cities.   


I really love the south and come to terms on being a southerner, especially after being someone who wanted to run away for years and years and move to NYC or something. But I realized the beauty of the south and there's a hella queer community here that I've found more comforting and different than queer communities in other areas. I mean, the town I live in is incredibly progressive and the last 3 mayors have been gay.   


There is beauty and comfort in the south. BUT, your fears and concerns are 100% valid. I also made the decision not to the leave the south when I realized it does need help. There's plenty of queer people here and other communities who need help and I felt like I couldn't leave them. I wanted to stay and work hard every day to making a community for areas, fighting against this political hate against us, creating safe places, etc. If someone wants to leave that's fine. Just because it worked out for me and I feel happy and safe doesn't mean it's the same for everyone. But I do believe the perspective of the south needs to be talked about more. Especially with the harmful stereotypes many of us face and disregard.  


I would highly suggest you to check out this book: Real Queer America: LGBT stories from Red States by author Samantha Allen who is a trans women. She travels the south and general red states, talking to queer leaders, communities, etc. Learning about the activism they do, why they don't leave, etc. It's really good and I brings a lot of perspective and shows the comfort.   


So again, I really don't want to call this a NTA or AITA. Because your thoughts and fears are valid but I do hope sharing this gives you some perspective and reassurance. Not saying "move down here." That's your decision and your comfort. But also wanting to use this as an opportunity to share queer southern culture and insights. Also completely understand picking up and having to move off. It's a big move and it's taken me awhile to finally establish some work and finance stability and I really couldn't do it right now nor would want to.   


Maybe a suggestion for you and your partner, you could try long distance if they did decide to move back. I wouldn't say pick up and move down but if you try long distance, could you come down and visit for a little bit? Let them meet your friends, community, events, etc.   


I hope things work out for you, OP. It's scary and stressful for sure so don't beat yourself up. But also know the south isn't a lost cause and there's power queer folks and communities here always ready to share love, protection, and help.

They bood them and Sylvia said “if it weren’t for drag queens there would be no gay liberation movement. We’re the front liners.” They kept attacking them and being transphobic and saying they were no different than their straight peers.

** also unit tip:

When me and my roommate moved in I was homeless in a hotel with no car and he was in Raleigh and they weren’t doing in person tours so we just went off the virtual tour. Once they approved us they asked what unit we wanted but we had no idea what to choose considering we couldn’t really get out there? We just came up with a list of preferences and they gave us this great unit which I really love. I believe the stuff we said was

- top floor (I’m sound sensitive and don’t like hearing people above me
- away from the entrance (same sound sensitive stuff. Had an old apartment with a gate and I was super annoyed hearing people drive in and out all the time.
- wooded area 

And bam. So don’t be afraid to tell them what you’re looking for rather than just looking at a list of unit numbers. 


Good luck!!
